idiom_name: slice assignment from a comprehension: l[:] = [x for x in l if keep(x)]
implementation_notes: Python lists own their length, but their per-element removal primitives are the expensive half of the idiom: del l[k], l.pop(k) and l.remove(v) are documented as O(n-k) because every following element shifts, so removing k values in a loop is O(n*k) and the while x in l: l.remove(x) form is quadratic. The single-pass equivalent is a comprehension or filter assigned back through the slice - l[:] = [x for x in l if keep(x)] - which builds the survivors once and replaces the list's contents in place, so every alias sees the new contents and the object's identity is preserved; l = [...] instead rebinds the name and leaves other references pointing at the old list. For membership tests, filtering through a set is the usual companion; collections.deque does not help, because arbitrary-position removal from a deque is still linear.
code_sketch:
sessions = [s for s in sessions if not s.expired]      # rebinds: aliases keep the old list
sessions[:] = [s for s in sessions if not s.expired]   # in place: same object, one pass
sessions[:] = filter(lambda s: not s.expired, sessions)  # same, with the builtin
pitfalls: The slice-assignment form and the rebinding form look interchangeable but are not: l = [...] silently detaches every other reference, and the old list keeps the removed elements alive.
Removing inside a for loop over the same list skips elements because the iterator's index advances past the shift; building the kept list first is the fix, which is precisely why the idiom exists.

filter() returns an iterator in Python 3: l[:] = filter(pred, l) works, but l = filter(pred, l) leaves an exhausted iterator whose indexing breaks - and a generator assigned to a slice is materialised anyway.

list.remove raises ValueError when the value is absent (so retry loops need a guard), removes only the first occurrence, and removal from tuples or strings is impossible: immutable sequences always take the copy-out path.
sources: docs.python.org, 5. Data Structures - list methods (remove removes the first matching item and raises ValueError when absent) and list comprehensions ('create a subsequence of those elements that satisfy a certain condition'): https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/datastructures.html

docs.python.org, Time complexity of operations on built-in types - delete item (del l[k]) and insert are O(n-k) per operation, while set slice (l[i:j] = t) costs O(n-i+len(t)): https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/time-complexity.html
